title: Pregnancy, Antenatal Classes & Preparing for Birth
description: Foetal development through pregnancy, the value of antenatal classes, birth choices and preparing a birth plan.
content_html:
Stages of Pregnancy and Foetal Development

Pregnancy lasts approximately 40 weeks, measured from the first day of the last menstrual period, and is divided into three trimesters. The first trimester (weeks 1-12) is the period of the most rapid and critical development. By the end of week 8, the embryo — now called a foetus — has all its major organs beginning to form (organogenesis), a beating heart, developing limb buds and emerging facial features. By 12 weeks, the foetus is around 6 cm long. Because organogenesis happens in the first trimester, this is the period when the baby is most vulnerable to teratogens (harmful substances such as alcohol, cigarette smoke and certain medications) that can disrupt organ formation.

The second trimester (weeks 13-27) is often described as the most comfortable stage for the mother. The foetus grows rapidly and movements (known as quickening) are felt by the mother from around 18-20 weeks. By 24 weeks, the foetus reaches the threshold of viability — the point at which a baby born prematurely has a chance of surviving with intensive medical support. The lungs are still immature at this stage. The third trimester (weeks 28-40) is characterised by rapid weight gain, further development of the brain, and the maturation of the lungs. The foetus turns head-down (cephalic presentation) in preparation for birth, usually by 36 weeks. The average birth weight at term is around 3.3 kg (7.3 lb).

Key Fact

The term ‘threshold of viability’ refers to 24 weeks of pregnancy — the point at which a premature baby may survive with intensive neonatal care. Before 24 weeks, the lungs are too undeveloped to support breathing without the placenta. This is also the legal limit for abortion in the UK under the Abortion Act 1967.

The Value of Antenatal Classes

Antenatal classes (also known as parentcraft classes) are educational sessions designed to prepare expectant parents for labour, birth and the immediate postnatal period. In the UK, they are offered through the NHS (typically via the midwifery team) and by independent organisations such as the National Childbirth Trust (NCT). Classes typically cover: the stages of labour and what to expect; pain relief options (including breathing techniques, water, TENS machines, gas and air, epidurals); infant feeding, including the benefits of breastfeeding and practical guidance on formula feeding; newborn care (nappy changing, bathing, safe sleeping); and emotional wellbeing and postnatal mental health.

Research consistently shows that parents who attend antenatal classes feel more confident and less anxious about labour. Classes also serve a social function — many parents form lasting support networks with others at a similar stage, reducing the isolation that can accompany new parenthood. Partners are encouraged to attend because an informed birth partner can provide effective practical and emotional support during labour. The main limitation of NHS classes is that they are often delivered in a single session or block and may not suit everyone's schedule; independent NCT classes are more comprehensive but carry a cost.

Choices for Where to Give Birth

In the UK, women with uncomplicated pregnancies are offered a genuine choice about where they give birth. The three main options are: a hospital consultant-led maternity unit, which offers the full range of medical interventions (epidurals, continuous foetal monitoring, theatre for caesarean sections) and is recommended for high-risk pregnancies; a midwife-led unit (MLU) or birth centre, which provides a homelike environment staffed by midwives with access to pain relief including water pools, without routine medical intervention — transfer to a hospital may be needed if complications arise; and a home birth, attended by two community midwives, which is suitable for women with straightforward pregnancies who wish to give birth in their own environment. Evidence from the Birthplace in England study (2011) showed that for low-risk women planning a second or subsequent birth, home and MLU settings are as safe as hospital settings for the baby, with lower rates of intervention.

Women have a range of pain relief options during labour. Non-pharmacological methods include water (hydrotherapy in a birth pool), which buoyancy and warmth can significantly reduce pain; TENS machines (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation), which send mild electrical pulses to interfere with pain signals; breathing and relaxation techniques; and massage from a birth partner. Pharmacological methods include Entonox (gas and air — a 50/50 mix of nitrous oxide and oxygen, inhaled through a mouthpiece), which takes the edge off pain without full pain relief; pethidine (an opioid injection that reduces pain and promotes relaxation but can cause drowsiness in the baby if given close to birth); and the epidural, which is an injection of local anaesthetic into the epidural space in the lower back providing effective pain relief from the waist down, available only in hospital settings. Women discuss and note their preferences in their birth plan but can change their mind during labour.

The Birth Plan

A birth plan is a document that expectant parents prepare, usually in the third trimester, outlining their wishes and preferences for labour and birth. A birth plan might cover: the preferred place of birth; who will be present as a birth partner; pain relief preferences; preferred positions for labour and birth; whether the mother wishes to have continuous foetal monitoring or intermittent auscultation; preferences regarding cord clamping (delayed cord clamping allows blood to continue transferring from the placenta to the baby after birth); and feeding intentions (breastfeeding or formula). A birth plan is not a rigid contract — midwives and medical staff will always prioritise the safety of mother and baby — but it helps ensure the woman's wishes are known and respected as far as possible.

Key Fact

Delayed cord clamping — waiting at least one to three minutes before clamping and cutting the umbilical cord after birth — is now recommended by NICE (the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence) for all births where the baby does not need immediate resuscitation. It allows up to a third more blood volume to transfer from the placenta to the newborn, boosting iron stores and reducing the risk of anaemia in infancy.

Alongside emotional and educational preparation, parents need to make practical preparations before the baby arrives. A hospital bag should be packed from around 36 weeks and include clothing for the mother and baby, toiletries, feeding equipment (e.g. breast pads or a sterilised bottle and formula), the birth plan and maternity notes, a car seat for the journey home, and snacks. At home, a safe sleeping environment must be arranged: the safest place for a newborn to sleep is on their back, in their own separate sleep surface (cot, crib or Moses basket), in the same room as a parent for at least the first six months. The room temperature should be kept at around 16-20°C. These are the Lullaby Trust guidelines for reducing the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Financial and employment preparations are also important: statutory maternity pay in the UK begins at 26 weeks pregnant, and parents should notify employers and understand entitlements to shared parental leave well in advance.
exam_tip_html: Questions on antenatal classes often ask you to ‘evaluate the value’ or ‘discuss the benefits’ — make sure you cover both the educational benefits (knowledge of labour stages, pain relief, infant feeding) and the social benefits (support networks, reduced anxiety), then challenge with limitations (accessibility, cost of NCT, single-session NHS provision). For birth plan questions, always include the point that it is a guide rather than a guarantee, as safety takes priority over stated preferences. For questions on birth choices, name all three settings (hospital, MLU, home) and link each to an appropriate scenario.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pregnancy is divided into three trimesters: organogenesis and highest vulnerability to harm occurs in the first trimester; the threshold of viability is reached at 24 weeks; and lung maturation and final growth happen in the third trimester.
  • Antenatal classes prepare parents for labour, birth and newborn care, reducing anxiety and building peer support networks; birth choices include hospital, midwife-led unit and home birth, each suited to different risk profiles.
  • A birth plan records preferences for labour and birth and is shared with the midwife in advance; it guides rather than dictates care, as the safety of mother and baby always takes priority over stated wishes.

glossary_terms.definition: The term used for the developing baby from 8 weeks of pregnancy (approximately 6 weeks after fertilisation) until birth, when all major organs are present and further development is growth and maturation.
Sessions offered to expectant parents, typically in the third trimester, covering labour, birth, pain relief, infant feeding and newborn care to increase confidence and readiness.
A written record of a pregnant woman's preferences for labour, birth and the immediate postnatal period, shared with her midwife and birth partner in advance.
The point in pregnancy, at 24 weeks, at which a premature baby may survive with intensive neonatal medical support, as the lungs have developed sufficiently to have some chance of functioning.

practice_questions.text:
During which trimester does organogenesis (the formation of major organs) mainly take place?
A) First trimester (weeks 1-12)
B) Second trimester (weeks 13-27)
C) Third trimester (weeks 28-40)
D) Organogenesis occurs throughout all three trimesters equally
State two benefits for parents of attending antenatal classes.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: increased knowledge of labour stages and pain relief / increased confidence / reduced anxiety / guidance on infant feeding / newborn care skills / social support networks with other expectant parents / partner feels better prepared to support during labour. Both must be distinct. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what a birth plan is and why it is important in antenatal preparation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: a birth plan is a written document setting out a woman's preferences for labour and birth. 2 marks: it covers aspects such as pain relief preferences, who will be present, birth setting, and feeding intentions, and is shared with the midwife in advance. 3 marks: it is important because it ensures the woman's wishes are known and respected as far as possible, even if she is unable to communicate during labour, while also acknowledging that safety takes priority and plans may need to change. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the threshold of viability at 24 weeks. Explain one reason why the baby is at greater risk if born before this point.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): the threshold of viability is the point at which a premature baby born at 24 weeks may survive with intensive neonatal support, as the lungs have reached sufficient development to have some chance of functioning (2 marks for a clear, accurate description; 1 mark for a basic statement). Explanation (up to 2 marks): before 24 weeks the lungs are too immature to sustain breathing independently or with ventilator support, because the air sacs (alveoli) and surfactant (the substance that prevents air sacs from collapsing) have not yet developed sufficiently (2 marks for a developed explanation with a specific reason; 1 mark for a vague statement). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A first-time mother is 30 weeks pregnant and has been offered a place on an NHS antenatal class. She is unsure whether to attend, as she feels she can find all the information she needs online.

Discuss the benefits and limitations of attending antenatal classes compared with using online resources to prepare for birth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion. Benefits of classes: practical, interactive preparation (e.g. hands-on practice of nappy changing, breastfeeding positioning); real-time questions answered by a midwife; social networks formed with other parents due at the same time; partner involvement. Benefits of online resources: accessible at any time, often free, wide range of sources, can revisit information. Limitations of classes: may be infrequent, only one or two NHS sessions, may not match availability or learning style. Limitations of online: quality varies, risk of misinformation, no social element. A clear evaluative judgement should be reached.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant points explained with reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One point with a brief reason.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A pregnant woman with a straightforward, low-risk pregnancy is deciding whether to give birth in hospital, at a midwife-led unit, or at home.

Evaluate the extent to which a midwife-led unit is the best choice for a low-risk pregnant woman who values minimal medical intervention but wants professional support during labour.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that for a low-risk woman who values minimal intervention, an MLU offers a homelike environment with midwife-led care, access to a birth pool and other non-pharmacological pain relief, lower rates of medical intervention than hospital, and evidence of comparable safety outcomes for mother and baby (Birthplace in England, 2011). Counter-arguments: an MLU cannot provide an epidural, continuous electronic foetal monitoring or emergency surgery; transfer to hospital (by ambulance) takes time and can be distressing if complications arise unexpectedly. A home birth may be even less interventional but carries a marginally higher risk for first-time mothers. A clear, substantiated judgement is required.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two well-developed points with an attempt at a judgement and reference to the scenario.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but one-sided or without a clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: At what week of pregnancy does the foetus reach the threshold of viability in the UK?
Which organisation offers antenatal classes in the UK as an independent provider, usually at a cost to parents?
The developing baby is called a foetus from _____ weeks of pregnancy.
Delayed cord clamping is recommended because it allows additional _____ to transfer from the placenta to the newborn.
Match each birth setting to its key characteristic.
right: Attended by two community midwives; no transfer of care needed if all is well
Homelike environment with birth pool; no epidural available
Full range of medical interventions; recommended for high-risk pregnancies

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three trimesters of pregnancy and their week ranges?

flashcard_questions.a: The formation of all major organs, occurring mainly in the first trimester.
The mother first feeling the baby's movements, typically around 18-20 weeks.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a TENS machine do during labour?
flashcard_questions.a: It sends mild electrical pulses to interfere with pain signals from the uterus.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Entonox and what is it made of?
flashcard_questions.a: Gas and air; a 50/50 mix of nitrous oxide and oxygen inhaled through a mouthpiece.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the safest position for a newborn to sleep?
flashcard_questions.a: On their back, in their own sleep surface, in the same room as a parent.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Lullaby Trust promote?
flashcard_questions.a: Safe sleeping guidelines to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

flashcard_questions.q: What is delayed cord clamping and why is it recommended?
flashcard_questions.a: Waiting 1-3 minutes before cutting the cord to allow extra blood to transfer to the baby, boosting iron stores.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three main birth setting options in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: Hospital maternity unit, midwife-led unit (birth centre), and home birth.

flashcard_questions.q: Which birth setting is recommended for high-risk pregnancies?
What is the average birth weight of a baby born at full term?
Why is the first trimester the most critical period for avoiding teratogens?
flashcard_questions.a: All major organs are forming during this time and are most vulnerable to damage from harmful substances.
